complete.problem: Trace physical chemistry from exothermic and endothermic reaction profiles, through rate curves and the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, and Le Chatelier’s principle, to the catalyst-shifts-equilibrium trap.
complete.selfExplanation: Explain why the sign of ΔH is set by where the products sit rather than the height of the hump, why a steeper concentration-time curve means a faster reaction, why heating puts more molecules past Ea, how an equilibrium opposes a disturbance while Kc changes only with temperature, and why a catalyst leaves the equilibrium position unchanged.

steps.annotation: The heat change at constant pressure, ΔH: products minus reactants on a reaction profile - negative for exothermic, positive for endothermic.
steps.text: Step 1 (s1): Exothermic: products lie below reactants. Exothermic: products lie below reactants. Draw the reactants level, climb the activation-energy hump, then fall to the products: the enthalpy change is negative and heat leaves the system. Keep your student notes open at the enthalpy change definition for this scene.

steps.annotation: The minimum energy Ea a collision needs for reaction to occur: on a reaction profile it is the climb from the reactants level to the transition state.
steps.text: Step 2 (s2): Endothermic: products lie above reactants. Endothermic: products lie above reactants. The reaction absorbs heat, ΔH is positive, and it still clears an activation-energy barrier. Compare the two profiles side by side in your student notes before we move from energy to speed.

steps.annotation: How fast reactant concentration falls, rate = -Δ[R] / Δt: read from the gradient of a concentration-time curve, steeper meaning faster.
steps.text: Step 3 (s3): Rate curves: steeper means faster. Rate curves: steeper means faster. Rate is the fall in reactant concentration over time, and the gradient of the curve is the rate. Raise the temperature or add a catalyst and the curve steepens. Now try the rate reading on the worksheet in pairs.

steps.annotation: The spread of molecular kinetic energies at a temperature: most molecules sit near the average, and only the tail past Ea can react on collision.
steps.text: Step 4 (s4): Maxwell–Boltzmann: more molecules past Ea at higher T. Maxwell–Boltzmann: more molecules past Ea at higher T. Most molecules sit near the average energy and only the fast tail can react; heating flattens and shifts the distribution so that tail grows. Check the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution definition in your student notes, then look ahead to the exit ticket question on this scene.

steps.annotation: The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system where the forward and reverse rates are equal and concentrations stay constant.
steps.text: Step 5 (s5): Le Chatelier: the system opposes the change. Le Chatelier: the system opposes the change. Add nitrogen and the Haber mixture makes more ammonia; compress it and it shifts toward fewer gas moles. Kc itself only changes with temperature. Work the Kc calculation on the worksheet now, in pairs.

steps.annotation: A catalyst speeds the forward and reverse reactions equally: the position of equilibrium is unchanged. - the catalyst shortens the journey to equilibrium, it does not move the destination, and Kc is unchanged.
steps.text: Step 6 (s6): A common mistake: a catalyst shifts equilibrium. A common mistake: a catalyst shifts equilibrium. The animation grows both rate arrows by the same factor and the equilibrium bars never move: equilibrium arrives sooner, in the same place, with the same Kc. Finish the worksheet trap question now, then the exit ticket on your own - the first question revisits exactly this scene.

faded.problem: For H2 + Cl2 → 2 HCl, with bond enthalpies H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242 and H-Cl 431 kJ mol-1, what is the enthalpy change of the reaction?
faded.selfExplanation: The first step is shown. Say how the energy taken in to break bonds and the energy given out when bonds form are evaluated, then how ΔH = in - out is found, and state what the negative sign means.

steps.annotation: Bond enthalpies: H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242 and H-Cl 431 kJ mol-1, and ΔH = energy in to break bonds - energy out when bonds form.
steps.text: Step 1: identify the values: ΔH = in - out with H-H 436, Cl-Cl 242 and H-Cl 431 kJ mol-1.

steps.annotation: Add and multiply it out: in = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ mol-1 and out = 2 x 431 = 862 kJ mol-1.
steps.text: Step 2: evaluate the two totals: in = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ mol-1 and out = 2 x 431 = 862 kJ mol-1.

steps.annotation: Subtract: 678 - 862 = -184 kJ mol-1 - the negative sign means the products lie below the reactants on the reaction profile, as in scene s1.
steps.text: Step 3: read the landing: ΔH = 678 - 862 = -184 kJ mol-1, so the reaction is exothermic.

paired.problem: For H2 + I2 → 2 HI, with bond enthalpies H-H 436, I-I 151 and H-I 299 kJ mol-1, calculate the enthalpy change of the reaction.
paired.solution: In = 436 + 151 = 587 kJ mol-1; out = 2 x 299 = 598 kJ mol-1; ΔH = 587 - 598 = -11 kJ mol-1. The reaction is exothermic.
